speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Fisheries) :
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I at the very
outset of my remarks extend to the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) my hearty congratulations upon the highly creditable maimer in which he discharged the onerous duty imposed upon him in his capacity as financial critic of the opposition. While in the main I may disagree with the conclusions at which he arrived and particularly in one instance, nevertheless I wish to pay him this tribute.
In the course of his remarks my hon. friend was good enough to single me out for special attention in connection with one subject in particular which is of great importance particularly to the older people in the maritime provinces, that is old age pensions. At page 2291 of Hansard my hon. friend referring to that subject, is quoted as follows:
If I mistake not, my hon. friend the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes) made a statement that he would resign, I think within three months, if the old age pension bill were not brought in.
The first time I had heard a statement of that kind was at an earlier stage in this session -or it may have been at the special session -at the instance of my hon. friend from Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley). I am afraid my

hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth has unwittingly been led astray by having given heed to the remarks of the hon. member for Hants-Kings. Then, after I had made a prompt denial of the statement made by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) promptly came to the rescue of his esteemed friend and said that I had made the statement that if 99 per cent of the old age pensions were not granted within three months I would resign. After the statement by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough I did not wish to interrupt the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth but since that hon. member was good enough to indicate that I had not denied the mild impeachment by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough I promptly made denial of that statement also. Whereupon my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough accepted my explanation. I submit in passing however that he did so within neither the letter nor the spirit of the rule. As a matter of fact I think my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough was carried away with the conviction that I had made a statement of that character.
It seems to me that there should be no doubt as to my position in the matter of old age pensions because on numerous occasions the question was discussed by me in the legislature of Nova Scotia. In fact during the last campaign I think I discussed it upon at least twenty-five or thirty platforms in the province of Nova Scotia alone and upon at least three occasions I dealt with it over a maritime radio hook-up. For those reasons my position must have been made very clear to the people in the province of Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces as a whole. As a matter of fact the press reports of my utterances appeared and, if you please, one of them reached the eye of none other than the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) who was then Prime Minister. Not only did he deign to notice my remarks, but he did me the signal honour of paying his respects to me by dealing with them in his opening speech in his maritime campaign in the city of St. John.
As a matter of fact my method of treatment of that subject was this: I always called in question the merits of the suggestion of my right hon. friend that it was contrary to the constitution for the Dominion of Canada to pay 100 per cent of old age pensions. I may say, with all deference to my right hon. friend, that I never took very much stock in that argument. Indeed, I subscribe to the state-

The Budget-Mr. Rhodes
ment of Premier Brownlee, of the province of Alberta, who said:
I have no patience with the argument that falls back on the British North America Act in this matter of dominion responsibility. If there is mutual agreement between the provinces and the dominion, who is there to object? Certainly none of the provinces will do so.
That was an utterance -which came from a source which could not be regarded as unfriendly to my right hon. friend, because, as a matter of fact, Premier Brownlee was one of the premiers to whom my right hon. friend was prepared to pay even a five cent piece. But the argument which I took in the course of that whole campaign, and the position which I took in the house, was this: If the constitution stands in the way, it did so in the case of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. That was an act which had been in force in this country for years and in virtue of which strikes and proposed strikes had been dealt with throughout the length and breadth of Canada for many years. But that act was called into question; the matter finally went on appeal to the Privy Council and was there declared ultra vires. But the dominion and the provinces thereupon did what I regard as a very sensible thing. They got together and came to an agreement in virtue of which every province passed a statute making the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act the law in its specific province. The man who is fond of the constitution might immediately rise and say: That course itself is ultra vires. Even so, what boots it to raise that point? Who is there to object? The dominion is in agreement; the provinces are in agreement, and the law is functioning
I submit in all deference that course should have been taken in connection with old ago pensions if the constitution is what stood in the way. Carrying my argument a little further, I made this statement: If it is a question of the constitution and not a question of amount; if it is constitutional for the dominion to pay 50 per cent of old age pensions, why not 60 per cent, or 70 per cent, or 99 per cent? And that 99 per cent was what caught the eye of the present leader of the opposition. Because in his speech at St. John he said he was "amazed and amused'' at the remarks of Premier Rhodes of Nova Scotia when he suggested that the dominion should pay 99 per cent of old age pensions. I never advocated that the dominion should pay it, but in the course of my argument I followed it up to that point and I think the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) went astray in following his leader who had also gone astray.
My right hon. friend, the present leader of the opposition, in his treatment of this subject in the maritime provinces, indulged in one of those characteristic performances of political fancy-skating on thin ice because, following that meeting in St. John, he spoke in the city of Charlottetown which is in the one province in Canada where he had to treat the subject very gingerly, the reason being that in that province is the largest number of aged persons and the treasury of the province is least able to stand the expenditure. Furthermore he was in a province which had a so-called Liberal administration, and so in speaking on that question in Charlottetown- and I say this advisedly because I listened to my right hon. friend over the radio-he said this:
The Conservatives say if they are returned to office they are prepared to pay 100 per cent old age pensions.
And then this is what my right hon. friend said:
I am prepared to consider payment by the dominion subject to an accounting with the provinces.
That was one of those delightfully and beautifully indefinite statements which are so characteristic of my right hon. friend. And it is capable of numerous interpretations, because it must be borne in mind if he meant the province was to contribute, he knew he was speaking in a province which through its government had said it could not contribute, but it must also be borne in mind that statement was made in conjunction with the proposal of the Conservative party that it would pay the whole of the old age pensions. I suggest that the clear inference which was left in the mind of the person who did not think that sentence out, in the province of Prince Edward Island in particular, was that my right hon. friend was holding out a hope they would pay old age pensions in full, especially when one bears in mind the fact that in Prince Edward Island my right hon. friend never raised the constitutional question at all.
But the next night he spoke in Sydney, Nova Scotia, and there he was in an entirely different atmosphere. There was a Tory government. He had none of those ham'per-ing influences which had held him down so closely the night before in Charlottetown. So the constitution was a real issue and in his speech in Sydney he stressed the constitution. He said: The law officers of the crown have advised me that the dominion cannot pay the whole of old age pensions, and if you want old age pensions in this province you must look to Premier Rhodes. No further
The Budget,-Mr. Rhodes

comment need be given as to the comparative methods of treatment of that subject by my right hon. friend first in Prince Edward Island, and next in Nova Scotia under their different conditions.
In the house this session my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition has taken very high ground with regard to the dangers involved in making political appeals for support because of special grants to the provinces. Last year this developed into a vicious principle. This year my right hon. friend has softened it down to an unsound principle. But in all seriousness I submit that what viciousness and unsoundness attach to the proposals of old age pensions and what improper method of political appeal has followed them are largely, if not entirely, due to my right hon. friend. He must assume full responsibility and I shall give reasons for having made that statement.
In connection with other grants over and above the regular subsidies to the provinces, what may be called special grants, for example, the Agricultural Instruction Act of 1913, the Employment Offices Coordination Act of 1918, the Canada Highways Act of 1919 and the Technical Education Act of 1919, every one of those acts was brought into force but with the full and expressed approval of every province in Canada, so I submit that in connection with those grants there cannot be any suggestion of improper method of political appeal. But what did my right hon. friend do in connection with old age pensions? Did he seek conferences? Did he seek agreement with the provinces? Upon the eve of an election, spurred on for reasons, which I shall not enter into at the moment, my right hon. friend not only did not have the agreement of the provinces, but in the case of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec he had the explicit promise, given in advance by Premier Ferguson and Premier Taschereau that their provinces would have nothing to do with the proposals of my right hon. friend.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister will pardon me; it wa3 just after the election, not on the eve of the election.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My time is too 'limited to enter into any controversy with my hon. friend, but my statement is substantially correct. In the case of Nova Scotia a communication was sent with regard to the attitude of the province, and the province said it was not in a position to enter into such an arrangement. The point I desire to make, however, is that if there has been any improper method of political appeal through grants of this kind, my right hon. friend the leader of the op-TMr. Rhodes.]
position and his friends must assume full and sole responsibility. If political appeal, rather than the welfare of the public, had been in our minds, we had an opportunity to pursue that course with the technical education measure which is before the house at the present time. If we had desired to play politics we could have deferred consideration of that proposal for two or three years, until the eve of an election, when we might get some political benefit from it, but we did not do so. It has been brought down at the first regular session of parliament, and by the time an election comes along it will be taken for granted and any political effect will have been lost. That will show that we had in mind as a government not the party welfare but the welfare of the public who, through this measure, will participate pro rata in the sum of $750,000 per year.
Just one word with regard to my attitude in connection with old age pensions. I am fully pledged to the full payment of old age pensions by this government. This government is pledged to the payment of old age pensions by the dominion, and the Conservative party is so pledged. If this session had been held during even normal times there is no question but that this pledge would have been implemented in full but, Mr. Speaker, the thinking public at large know that we are passing through a world economic upheaval, and that it would have meant very heavy additional obligations upon the treasury of the country to have gone the full distance at this time. We have bridged half the gap; there remains but the final step of 25 per cent, and I submit that this step will be taken as soon as sound financing will permit.
There is one other subject arising out of this debate to which I feel I must briefly but especially allude. My hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) had a word to say about the Canadian National Railways. Let me say in parentheses that if there is one hon. member of this house whose utterances are invariably fair, conciliatory and mild, it is my hon. friend from North Waterloo. Therefore any remarks he makes have attached to them perhaps a greater significance than would follow in the case of some hon. members who are perhaps not so careful in what they say. Furthermore, there attaches to his utterances also a further significance by reason of the fact that for a number of years he was a minister of the crown. During the course of his speech he made particular reference to the attitude of the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) on the subject of the Canadian National Railways, and those who heard the hon. member for Stanstead are of course aware

The Budget-Mr. Rhodes
of the fact that he uttered his views in no uncertain terms. Then my hon. friend from North Waterloo, by inference at all events, endeavoured to make it appear that the Prime Minister, as head of the government, was identified with the views expressed by the hon. member for Stanstead. The first statement of the hon. member for North Waterloo was that the Prime Minister was not sympathetic to the Canadian National Railways in his utterances, and then follows a paragraph which appears at page 2487 of Hansard, having reference to the remarks Of the hon. member for Stanstead:
I felt that some of us who are the friends of public ownership, as exemplified in the operation of the national railways, would take issue with him on that point and say to him that if he represents the opinion of the government, and if what he said indicates that in any sense this is merely the preliminary of a propaganda against the national railways, they are playing with fire.
Then he starts his very next sentence with these words:
These attacks upon the national railways . . .
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in the opening portion of the first paragraph my hon. friend from North Waterloo sets himself up as a friend of public ownership, in contradistinction to those to whom he was referring on this side of the house, and I wish to direct your attention particularly to the fact that while he might have been justified, in referring to the remarks of the hon. member for Stanstead only, in using the words "this attack," he did not do so; he used the words "these attacks on the national railways." That still further tended to leave the implication that he was coupling up the Prime Minister and the government of this country with the utterances of the hon. member for Stanstead. Let me say now that I attribute no ulterior or unfair motive to my hon. friend from North Waterloo, but that seems to be the implication.
I desire not only to take exception to that implication, but to repudiate in the strongest possible terms any such suggestion and to assert positively that it is without foundation. I am sure my hon. friend from North Waterloo and his leader would have been the first to take exception if, during the last session under the previous government, hon. members on the other side of the house had fastened the responsibility upon the then government for the utterances of my hon. friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), when he made attacks upon the premier of the province of Quebec. They would have been equally justified in that instance as was my hon. friend from North Waterloo in attempting to make
the utterances of my hon. friend from Stanstead the utterances of the government.
What are the facts? In addition to having raised hundreds of millions of dollars for capital expenditures in connection with our railways, to-day parliament is called upon to provide annually for the Canadian National Railways, for maintenance and improvements, a greater sum of money than was necessary for the whole cost of government in this country only a few years ago. Is this government or this parliament, or any government or parliament, which may hereafter inquire, as it is the duty of parliament to inquire, into the financial position of the Canadian National Railways, to be charged with making an attack on public ownership? Either the expenditures in connection with the Canadian National Railways are sound or they are not. If they are sound, no examination can do injury; if on the other hand they are unsound, even in part, then parliament owes a duty to the people of Canada to apply the necessary remedies. It would be unfortunate indeed, both for the railways and for the country, if the Canadian National Railways were to be regarded as sacrosanct. Many a child has been spoiled through over indulgence and lack of control on the part of fond parents, and in the interests of the Canadian National Railways it is our duty to scrutinize expenditures with the utmost care and, where it is necessary, to exercise a reasonable check and control. Hon. members of this house may have their own views upon the subject of private versus public ownership, but whether we agree with the one principle or the other, the fact is that we have government ownership. All parties are in agreement that it must be preserved and maintained. And it is the duty of all governments, of whatever political complexion, or whatever their views upon private or public ownership, to recognize facts and not to permit their sympathy to override sound business judgment in the matter of railway expenditures. As a last word upon this subject, may I express the fervent hope that in all our relationships with the Canadian National Railways, both now and in the future, it shall not be made the subject of party political controversy to the detriment of this great undertaking.
I regret that the limited time at my disposal will not permit me to traverse in detail, as I should like, the speech of my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth which covered some two and a half hours in time. At the certain risk of criticism-in fact, I predict now that I shall be criticized-for not having dealt with
25G8
The Budget-Mr. Rhodes

this, that or the other subject, I propose to treat with but one subject on this occasion, leaving other matters to be dealt with as opportunity presents itself. That subject is the coal policy. I think I can best make a proper entry into that subject by taking the house back to the conditions found in the coal mining areas in the province of Nova Scotia, following that great strike which ended in the early summer of 1925.
That I deal with Nova Scotia perhaps to a greater extent than with other coal producing areas in the dominion is because I happen to know the conditions there better. But what I say with respect to conditions touching that province will in the main hold good in relation to the coal industry in other provinces of the dominion. I shall not go into gruesome detail regarding all the suffering and distress and disaster which followed that eventful strike. I make reference to this merely for the reason that the underlying root cause for that strike and for the distress in that industry was the lack of regular employment-the lack of continuous employment. That strike was settled by way of compromise, and one of the conditions of that settlement was an agreement on the part of the government of Nova Scotia that it would appoint a royal commission to inquire into all conditions surrounding the coal industry. That commission was presided over by Sir Andrew Duncan. It is sometimes lo9t sight of that there were two Duncan commissions. Another member of that commission of three was Mr. Hume Cronyn, of London, Ontario, once an honoured member of this house and a very highly esteemed and much respected citizen of that province.
Now, in the addendum to the report brought down by that commission, covering several pages, Mr. Cronyn makes certain statements- not findings-with respect to that industry.
I have not time to read at length from it but I must quote at least one or two paragraphs. He says'.
The commission as a whole did not feel* warranted in expressing their opinion on some of the remedies suggested for relief of the coal industry in Nova Scotia. These remedies touched on matters within both provincial and dominion control, and of necessity involved a pronouncement on questions which for more than a generation have been the subject of political discussion.
The chairman of the commission, coming as he does from Great Britain, did not fcsl like entering upon findings; he dealt with a subject, which was more or less domestic in its character. I would direct the attention

of the house to these significant lines of one paragraph:	.
It will appear from our report that one, perhaps the greatest, cause of distress and discontent is due to irregularity of employment in the mines.
I would ask the house to listen to these two paragraphs:
I f, then, we of the central provinces are unwilling to sacrifice something of our prosperity on the altar of common citizenship to aid, perhaps indeed to save, the main industry of Nova Scotia, we may witness an estrangement of far-reaching consequences; for it is not exaggerating the situation to say that the inhabitants of the maritime provinces are in a frame of mind that insists upon relief from the disadvantages under which they labour. My appeal then, to my friends (if I may so term them), of Quebec and Ontario, and through them to the parliament of Canada, is on the highest ground of national unity. Let us, overlooking the pecuniary sacrifices involved, take the necessary measures to safeguard the welfare of our brothers by the sea.
Now, I do not recite passages in order to lend any emphasis to the conditions of which Mr. Cronyn spoke at that time, but merely for the purpose of emphasizing the importance of this industry to that section of the country. I have read these passages for that purpose and for no other. Bear in mind that from one-fifth to one-fourth of the whole industrial life of Nova Scotia is dependent upon its mines. To give an idea of the relative magnitude of the industry, let me say that half of the workmen's compensation paid in that province comes from the Dominion Steel and Goal Company in this mining area alone.
I do not propose-I have not sufficient time-to deal with the causes leading up to the appointment of the second Duncan commission, but I will cite one paragraph from the report of that commission. Bearing in mind that not only did it have as its chairman Sir Andrew Duncan, but that it included two other esteemed gentlemen, one of whom was my immediate predecessor in the portfolio I have now the honour to occupy, and the other a highly esteemed county court judge in Nova Scotia, whose political sympathies, before his elevation, were akin to the party of my hon. friends opposite I shall read what is stated on page 36 of the report of the Royal Commission on Maritime Claims:
We cannot too strongly emphasize the discouragement which the maritime provinces feel at the delay which has already taken place in giving practical shape to a policy which has been recommended so definitely by the Dominion Fuel Board as the only method by which eastern and central Canada can be relieved of the dependence upon imported anthracite. The difficulty in the Nova Scotia coal field is to keep winter employment regular.

The Budget-Mr. Rhodes
Even a partial displacement of the anthracite imported for domestic uses would provide an outlet for their coal, with definite prospects of growth and permanence, and having the very-great advantage that it would increase and make regular their winter employment.
Now just a word in order that we may-grasp the situation as respects the coal industry in Canada as a whole. We have to-day in Canada mines developed and equipped and in a position to operate, capable of producing a total of 28,550,000 tons of coal per annum, located as follows: Nova Scotia, 8,000,000; British Columbia, 2,500,000; Alberta, 17,000,000; Saskatchewan, 750,000; New Brunswick, 300,000. At the same time we operated those mines last year to just a trifle over 50 per cent of their capacity. I cannot attempt to depict to the house what it means to try to operate an industry of that character only half time. At the same time we imported into Canada 18,079,200 tons of fuel. We imported anthracite to the extent of 4,254,500 tons; we imported 1,048,000 tons of coke from the United States and 12,700 tons from Great Britain. We imported ' 1.3,218,000 tons of bituminous coal, which included a small amount of lignite from the United States, and 146,000 tons from Great Britain. These figures make up the total of 18,679,200 tons which I have mentioned already, which figure includes coal, both bituminous and anthracite, coke and a small amount of lignite. I have lumped them together in one figure-

speechtext: Could the minister give the house the distribution in Canada of those importations?

speechtext: My hon. friend means the distribution of the various quantities?

speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That would be a very large order and as a matter of fact I have not the details before me.
To put it another way, it means that if our coal mines had operated last year one hundred per cent of their existing capacity, we would have had to import during the year of 1930, which was not a high consumption year, no less than 5,007,200 tons of coal in order to meet our requirements. That is a simple statement of fact. It protrays a situation which requires no elaborate comment. Our problem in Canada is to increase the production of Canadian mines to a point of continued production with consequent regular employment. I submit that that problem constitutes a direct challenge to members of governments in Canada, both provincial and dominion, and to the executive capacity of
those engaged in business, in transportation and in industry. I will not overlook the difficulties of transportation nor the obstacles imposed by geography, but at the same time I am convinced in my own mind that this problem is capable of solution.
In approaching the consideration of this problem I would respectfully ask the attention of those who are opposed to tariffs, particularly as they apply to industries which might be regarded as exotic, as not indigenous or even adaptable to this country; I submit that we have here an industry which is native in being and important, and therefore one which requires our serious consideration for its welfare.
So far as I have been able to ascertain there never has been a country in the history of the world which has been great industrially unless its industry has been based upon coal. That statement may be subject to some modification owing to hydro-electric development and the larger use of oil, but I think it will be found that that statement holds substantially good even under these conditions.
Let me refer again to the report of the royal commission, known as the second Duncan commission. I am speaking now particularly to those who have not a kindly feeling towards tariffs. This commission was presided over by Sir Andrew Duncan, who was an adherent of the Manchester Liberal school and was not one predisposed in favour of tariffs. The commission stated that for reasons which had been pointed out to them, to the effect that the matter was under consideration by the tariff advisory board, they would not make a specific finding in the matter of tariffs, .but they did say this:
But we may be permitted to say that we are impressed with the need for reconsideration of the customs tariff in its relation to coal, anthracite and coke, and we recommend that the Tariff Advisory Board should be asked to give immediate consideration to the subject.
I have no desire to interject into my argument with respect to this coal question any political considerations, but I think it would be -fair for me bo say that this report was brought down over four and one-half years ago and that so far as hon. gentlemen opposite are concerned, during the whole period of their tenure of office they made no effort to give heed to the recommendation of their own commission which pointed out that immediate consideration of the subject was imperative.
Hon. members who heard the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth make his very excellent speech will recall that he coasted along very freely until he came to the coal proposals. He bore down very heavilv in his
The Budget-Mr. Rhodes

arguments upon every other phase of his criticism, but he treated the coal proposals very gingerly, in fact he might be said to have crossed the danger area with a hap, skip and jump. His first remark was that he did not propose to look a gift horse in the mouth, but I submit, sir, that here was a clear indication that there was a gift being made to the coal industry of Canada by means of these tariff proposals. He was as good as his word, he did not look the gift horse in the mouth; he spurned it out of hand, because he submitted an amendment which, if carried, would have the effect of denying to the people of his native province the opportunity of receiving the benefits contained in the proposals.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth during the course of his remarks made the statement that it had always been his humble endeavour to do what he could to advance the interests of the coal industry of the province of Nova Scotia. That may be so, but I would point out to the house that while my hon. friend was a minister of the crown, he was responsible in his own department for ordering coal for government services in the Department of National Defence during a period of years. Year after year my hon. friend submitted advertisements asking for tenders for coal to heat the various government buildings under the charge of his department, and what did he advertise for? Anthracite coal. In the year 1928-29 he purchased no less than 7,783 tons of anthracite coal, and in the year 1929-30, 8,535 tons. Perhaps that is not a great amount, but translated into terms of bituminous coal it means that last year his department purchased the equivalent of upwards of 10,000 tons of bituminous coal. Contrast the action of mv hon. friend in spite of his protestations, with the concrete actions of this administration. The moment we came into office we set up the policy that we would use none other than Canadian fuel in Canadian buildings, except in those isolated instances where it would be more advantageous to use imported coal.
I regret, Mr. Speaker, that I am advised that I have only two minutes left and I am only nicely started upon my remarks. This is my first experience of this closure rule, and hence the embarrassment in which I find myself. I shall endeavour to compress my remarks into the very smallest compass in view of the few minutes that remain to me.
Our proposals in regard to coal are, in the first place, a duty of 40 cents a ton on anthracite. I submit that that tax, which was held up as a burden plaoed upon the people of Ontario and Quebec, need not be paid at all by the people of those provinces. In the first
fMr. Rhodes.]
place, even if they buy anthracite coal, the treasury gets the benefit of the tax. It remains to be seen, however, how much of that tax will be paid by the producer. I venture to say, owing to the highly competitive nature of the business, that the larger portion, if not the whole of that tax, will be paid by the producer in the United States. But, sir, there is no reason in the world why the householder in Ontario and Quebec who is a large user of anthracite coal should use a pound of anthracite because we have in Canada to-day, in coke, a fuel that is infinitely superior to anthracite. Exhaustive tests have fully demonstrated that the man who uses, we will say, ten tons of anthracite in a year can save, in round figures, about S23.50 if he will use coke, which is a far superior fuel. You say: There is a duty of $1 per ton on coke. True, but the coke can be made in Canada. Even if the coke is made in this country from United States coal, there is a drawback of 99 per cent.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There should not be.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Cantley) says that there should not be. But the fact is that it is there. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth criticized us very severely the other day because tariff item 1049 had not been deleted. When he made that criticism it was not so ingenuous as it might sound. It reminded me of the position taken by President Cosgrave of the Irish Free State, who when taxed by Mr. De Valera with not having done something, replied, "They have burned down the buildings and now they complain to the government because there is a smell of smoke." My hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth and his friends are responsible for that tariff item 1049, and he expects us now to wipe it off out of hand. It is one thing to be responsible for the initiation of policies, and quite another thing to disturb settled conditions, after contracts have been entered into. That cannot be done overnight, but I agree with my hon. friend from Pictou that that item ought to be deleted, and I look forward to the time when it will be deleted.
If I may be permitted a moment just to conclude, it is not suggested that these proposals offer a complete solution of our problem of building up and maintaining a healthy and prosperous Canadian coal industry, but they do mark a great step forward in that direction, indeed, the greatest step forward in our history. It is not to be expected that their effects will be electric or immediate, but as a result of our policy I believe that we shall witness a gradual and steadily increasing

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot
improvement, and in the future our proposals can be revised and amended in the light of experience. Whatever may be said of this budget as a whole I have full faith that future generations will acclaim the proposals of the government and their contribution to our national development.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata):	Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to
listen to the "pro domo'' plea which my hon. friend the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes) has just made about old age pensions. He did not fail to speak about the five-cent piece, and I am not at all surprised, therefore, that he should be slated by the press for the Ministry, of Finance. As my hon. friends from the maritime provinces have repeatedly told me, the hon. member should lay a wreath on the grave of the former Minister of Finance, the late Mr. Robb, who paid subsidies to the province of Nova Scotia before they were due in order that the province should not have a deficit, and that was done not only for Nova Scotia but for New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island as well. My hon. friend said that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has given numerous interpretations of the Old Age Pension Act. Perhaps so, but I was very sorry to see the hon. Minister of Fisheries take the wrong one. He spoke about agreements with the provinces. There was a proposal submitted by the federal government to each of the provinces, and as soon as that proposal was accepted by a province, it was agreed to and the province was satisfied with it. My hon. friend complained about a statement that was made the other day by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) relating to the payment by the federal government of 99 per cent of the cost of the old age pension. Then, how is it that the Minister of Fisheries stated a moment ago that his own party is absolutely pledged to the full payment of the old age pensions.
The next matter which my hon. friend the Minister of Fisheries discussed was the Canadian National Railways, and in that connection he put me in company with the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett). He said that fond parents would not allow their children to be rude to one another, or something to that effect. But as I listened the other day to the remarks of my hon. friend from Stanstead I thought he was treating that child, the Canadian National Railways, pretty roughly, and I wondered if he was thinking of adopting another big fat and nice looking baby, the Canadian Pacific Railway. The hon. gentleman also said that he was in
favour of scrutinizing the affairs of the Canadian National Railways. In that we are in perfect accord, and I have now hope that in the near future I shall see the returns brought down which have been passed by the house and which I have repeatedly asked for. May I take this opportunity to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) for having been kind enough to bring down something yesterday, to give me a sweet mouth. I expect more in the near future.
There is another matter with which my hon. frend the Minister of Fisheries dealt and that is my relations with the premier of the province of Quebec. The hon. member (Mr. Short) who at the moment is presiding over the proceedings of this house

and I congratulate him upon the honour conferred upon him in being asked to take the chair-will, as one who has occupied a seat in the house for a number of years recall that I spoke about fair wages in the province of Quebec and also in the maritime provinces, and I gave a message to my good friend from Inverness (Mr. Macdougall) one day. I said to him:	Please give this message to the
premier of Nova Scotia, now the distinguished Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes). Tell him to take good care of the miners. See to it that their salaries are improved by a minimum wage law. I suppose that my hon. friend from Inverness had other things to do than to give that message, and I am very sorry he found it impossible to deliver it to the hon. Minister of Fisheries who at that time was the premier of the province to which I am referring. Hon. members may have noticed that lately they have not heard me speaking about the premier of the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, I shall state the
reason. I hear the Prime Minister say "Hear, hear." May I say to him that I have not been referring to the premier of the province of Quebec because his bad companion, Mr. Ferguson, has been sent to London. As the premier of Quebec is now in better company I have nothing to complain about. I wish to say further that after our efforts, our work and our complaints the payment to men working on the roads in the province of Quebec has been increased by 50 cents per day. Such an increase is appreciated by those labouring men and the increase represents a practice which to my knowledge has not been followed in the province of Nova Scotia. I am sure however that if my hon. friend the Minister of Fisheries had remained at his post as premier of the province of Nova
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot

Scotia he would have followed that good example of the province of Quebec. For that reason I am sorry he now holds a portfolio in this house. Concluding my remarks about the speech of the Minister of Fisheries, I have only one thing further to say. Although he represents a very fine constituency I am sorry he does not represent the capital city of the province of Nova Scotia owing to the fact that he has been the premier of that province. If sometime before prorogation the government decides to purchase the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon may I suggest that the present junior member for Halifax (Mr. Quinn) would be a proper representative for the new constituency of St. Pierre-Miquelon and the present Minister of Fisheries could take the seat of the' present junior member for Halifax.
Concerning coal I have very little to say. I wish to state however that if the duty on coal serves the purpose of helping the miner in the province of Nova Scotia, I am for it. If on the other hand it increases the cost of coal at the expense of the common people without offering a better chance to the miner I see no advantage in the change. Bituminous is a type of coal which is used in conjunction with a certain heating apparatus. The cost of the coal in addition to the expensive apparatus is too great for the pocket book of the poor man who is out of a job and who belongs to the great army of unemployed; as a result we seldom find those men using coke and bituminous coal for heating purposes. I am told however that many people in the maritime provinces use anthracite, as is done in other parts of the country.
As I wish to make my speech as short as possible I shall now direct my remarks to the promises made by the perpetual Tory candidate during the last election campaign in the constituency I have the honour to represent. Promise number one related to agriculture, and in the promise was included an upheaval of industry and further development of agriculture.
On May 29 the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Myers) said:
I may tell him,-
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr Beaubien).
-however, so far as the maritime provinces are concerned, that they cannot register as many complaints to the square inch as I have heard from western members this winter.
This is probably due to the good effect brought about by the implementing of the Duncan report by the Liberal government.

The hon. member said I looked like an honest-to-goodness farmer. May I at this time thank the hon. gentleman for that compliment. The fact that the leader of the opposition and hon. members on this side of the house look like farmers proves that hon. members of the Liberal party have identified themselves with the farmers and the workingmen of Canada. I was surprised when the hon. member for Queens, speaking of the east, made the following statement:
We are easy to deal with. When the price of butter is low we pocket our loss, and when it is high we take our profits and say nothing about it. It is easy to handle such a situation.
If hon. members were not accorded the privilege of bringing to parliament the farmers' grievances the functions of parliament would be better abolished. The farmers of my constituency are gentlemen, as are undoubtedly those of the constituency of my hon. friend from Queens and throughout the country. I was surprised therefore when looking at the Parliamentary Guide a few days ago to learn that the hon. member is a farmer. To my mind he did not show good manners when he stated that lawyers could not properly defend the case of the farmers. What about the right hon. leader of the government, one of the most distinguished members of the bar? The remarks of the hon. member constitute an insult lodged not only against the right hon. leader of his party but against all lawyers in the house, and 1 protest most strongly.
When the Prime Minister visited Riviere du Loup he addressed a very well attended meeting.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did the right hon. gentleman speak in the new station?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, he spoke about a mile from the station, but I may say I was glad to go to the station on his departure to wish him good luck. In the Gazette of July 14, I find the following:
Mr. Bennett spoke briefly of the necessity of inaugurating measures to help restore Canadian agriculture, dealt with the butter situation and said the issue was, whether Canada was to be a country or an annex. "Are you for Canada or some other country?" He asked: "Therein lies the issue. If you are for Canada, how can you help unless you send men to parliament who will pass laws to secure the markets of Canada for Canadians and give us an opportunity of selling our supplies abroad."
The practice of marketing abroad was a Liberal policy.
"Why," asked Mr. Bennett, "should eggs, meats, butter, cheese, et cetera be brought from abroad to feed Canadians?"

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot
Return No. 318 tabled on June 8 of this year disclosed the information that in spite of the fact that the tariff is higher now than it has ever been, the price of butter was lower in the month of May than it has been for twenty-seven years. I asked a question concerning the people who had tried to dump butter in the months of May, June and July prior to the election? That question appeared on the order paper, but was not answered and the information was not given. I asked the further question:
Who are the members of parliament who are or who have been directors, officers or members of the National Dairy Council since 1925?
I heard my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Thompson) say that he had been a member of the board, and I had been informed that he was not the only one on his side of the house. However the question to which I have referred was ruled out of order by Mr. Beau-chesne, Clerk of the House. May I take this opportunity to say that that gentleman has been quite severe concerning questions to be put on the order paper.
At this time I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) some questions. My first question is: How is it since less butter is imported the price is also less? Secondly: How is it that the price of milk and cream for home consumption remained about the same when the price of butter and cheese fell down? Third: How is it that the so-called protection policy does not protect the farmer at all?
During the election campaign several observations were made concerning pulpwood coming from Russia last year. At the special session my hon. friend from North Timiska-ming (Mr. Bradette) obtained an answer from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) concerning this importation of pulp-wood. The reply was as follows:
Pulpwood imports from Russia-Nothing. Construction wood imported from Russia- Nothing.	*
Until the special session our country had imported no pulpwood or construction wood from Russia; in spite of that fact however the government decided to place an embargo on all Russian products. The farmers in my constituency would be very much surprised if any good came from such an embargo. Last winter settlers, whose earnings are derived from the sale of lumber tried to sell pulpwood at $5 per cord, and their offers were refused.
As regards the question of the seasonal tariff on potatoes, the farmers in my part of the country are interested in raising potatoes.
The following order in council was published in the official gazette on May 5 last:
By order in council (P.C. 1033) dated the 1st May, 1931, order in council (P.C. 937) dated the 22nd April, 1931, was amended by deleting potatoes from the list of products which the Minister of National Revenue was thereby authorized to fix the value of, and the value for duty of potatoes fixed by the minister as contained in Appraiser's Bulletin No. 3704, dated the 22nd April, 1931, is cancelled.
Afterwards, in order to give an opportunity to the farmers, the government fixed the value of radishes, and later there are other orders in council for strawberries and cucumbers, but there is nothing for potatoes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, that is what it is
for.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are many ways of
helping the farmer. When I was elected, fences and ditches along the Intercolonial railway in my constituency were in bad shape, and through the good-will and intelligence of the then Minister of Railways, Mr. Dunning, who grasped the situation thoroughly, the law was changed in order that the Intercolonial might be put under the jurisdiction of the railway board in regard to operation. This work has since been done and I was glad to hear the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) say the other day that he would follow that wise policy. Amongst other things that were done, submarine telephone cables were laid in order that the farmers of distant parishes might have better communication across lakes and on islands in the St. Lawrence river, and many other works were carried out in order to help the farmer.
In regard to old age pensions, the Prime Minister came to Riviere du Loup and according to the Gazette this is what he said:
He renewed the pledge of the national Conservative convention at Winnipeg as regards old age pensions.
At this point may I relate something which is delightful. During the last campaign my opponent said: "How will the leader of our party succeed in having the old age pension
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot

paid in full by the federal government without any increase in debt, without any more expenditure?" He said, "It is very easy; he will cancel those legations at Tokyo, Washington and London." As regards the mention of Washington, that was surely a lack of foresight, and the same thing may be said of London, because Mr. Ferguson was sent there. My opponent said more than that. There was only one legation left, that of Paris, where Mr. Roy is. When a Conservative candidate returned to his home, he said to his wife: "I have been offered the appointment to succeed Mr. Roy." She said, "Who said that to you?" He said, "Mr. Dube." She said, "What Mr. Dube?" He replied, "The mayor of Riviere du Loup, who is to say a good word in my favour to Mr. Bennett and I might be appointed to Paris."
I quote again what my right hon. friend said at Riviere du Loup:
We propose to pass a law, the first session, to give Canadians a fair chance of competition on equal terms, a fair chance to develop Canada against competitors from any part of the world, said the leader.
This is the Liberal policy.
We propose to do that, the first session, or we will get out of office trying. I ask for your support and there is only one way of giving it -vote for Messrs. Dube and Audet, if you mean to help us build up Canada.
Not build up a station, but build up Canada.
Mr. King cut off the federal grant to aid agriculture; if we come back, we propose to renew that grant, for farmers have the right to know everything that science can teach them.
Let me refer to what was said during the election by my opponent about the Imperial conference. This is something which was also delightful. He said more than the leader of the party. He asked:	"Who are
the Conservatives who are to represent Canada at the Imperial conference?" He mentioned the present Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan), who did not go there; the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion), who also did not go and the Hon. Senator Chapais, who did not go there. One day he said to the people who were present: "Would you not like it better if I went there than he?" pointing to me. I replied: "I never mentioned it." But he was to go to the Imperial conference, and the day before the election he said: "This is the last time I come before you as a private citizen. The next time I appear before you I will be Minister of Labour." I wonder if it is because he has changed his mind that the Prime Minister has asked Senator Robertson, who is a very good man, to take that portfolio.

With regard to the transcontinental railway the speech of the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) on June 5 of this year was answered on July 12 of last year by the Prime Minister when he came home. The hon. member for Stanstead said, as reported in Hansard at page 2348:
How far that eloquent chieftain-
Speaking of Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
-of this parliament was able to lead the people astray when he engaged in public ownership.
This is how the Prime Minister replied, when speaking at Riviere du Loup last July:
Mr. Bennett drew cries of "Shame" from the audience when he contrasted Premier Mackenzie King with Laurier. When the United States had threatened to cut Canada off boundary privileges, Laurier had declarfed that Canada would build two railways of her own. But when protection was asked against American imports, Mr. King had said: "Hush, do not provoke the United States."
The present leader of the opposition is alive; he has to be fought; but Sir Wilfrid Laurier is dead and he has what he deserves -praise.
It must be remembered that the grades were changed under the Borden administration by people who wanted to destroy the work of Laurier and this is why the transcontinental railway did not serve the purpose it was intended to serve. In my constituency some of the grades are so bad, they have to cut trains in two in order that they may pass with heavy loads.
There was a promise of a junction between Riviere du Loup and the transcontinental railway, but I have heard nothing about it since this pamphlet of promises which I hold in my hand was published.
There is a promise about the development of harbour facilities at Riviere du Loup. I have here the program of the Conservative candidate in my constituency which contains this promise, but according to a certified copy of a resolution that was passed by the municipal council of the city of Riviere du Loup on April 13 last, he voted against it. His party voted not only against it, but against the consideration and study of the matter by experts. This is shown by the report of the vote on page 1031 of Hansard.
With regard to the improvement of the railway shops, I have an order for return dated April 23, in which appears letters from the Conservative candidate, as mayor of Riviere du Loup, to the director of unemployment and to other people, saying that before January 1, owing to his own ignorance, the city of Riviere du Loup did not pay

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot
regular wages or observe regular working hours ^ for the men on the pay list. The Tory candidate was promising better wages and fair hours of work to the workingmen, but he did not even act according to the regulations of the Unemployment Relief Act.
Just a word with regard to the employees of the Canadian National Railways. On June 1, at page 2199 of Hansard, I asked:
1.	Is it the intention of the Canadian National Railways to reinstate Mr. Noel Plourde, ex-conductor?
2.	If so, when?
The Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) said, "Answered," but my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) said:
Mr. Speaker, this question reads; "Is it the intention of the Canadian National Railways to reinstate Mr. Noel Plourde." Surely we have reached the stage where such a question should not be asked.
Mr. Pouliot: I should not like to ask a question which causes discomfort to the cabinet.
Mr. Manion: The cabinet has nothing at all to do with the question.
The point is that the Minister of Railways was ready to answer; he had received the answer from the Canadian National Railways, but my right hon. friend prevented him from giving the answer to Hansard.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
For the information of
the hon. gentleman I may say that the answer would have been that the matter was in the hands of the railway and not in the hands of the government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I understand that very
well, but the answer came from the railway to the minister, and the minister was acting in accordance with the answer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, that was the answer of the railway; they were not going to disclose their business.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad my right hon. friend is giving the answer to-day; it was worth speaking about.
There is also another matter, with regard to the appointment of workingmen on the recommendation of the Conservative candidate, on the ship Mikula, which is operated by the Department of Marine. One of these men was convicted for stealing apples, so I would ask the Minister of Marine if he has insured the furniture of the ship against theft, or if he intends to use the ship as a galley for convicts or ex-convicts. I have a copy of the judgment in the case, the minister is not here, but I will send it to him to-night. This man who was recommended, took the place of other people with a better record.
Now I come to a very dear subject, the Riviere du Loup station. Speaking in Brandon, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister made a statement with which I entirely agree, except for the blame which he tries to place on the previous administration; as an enunciation of principle his statement is perfect. He said:
I want to say that the Conservatives in power will give the Canadian National management a stronger support, and a more disinterested support, than they have had under the King administration.
If the right hon. gentleman had said s strong and disinterested support, and left it at that, I would have agreed with him entirely. He continued:
There will be less log-rolling and interference; the management will be better able to carry out their policies without politicians butting in and trying to stop them.
I have in my hands a copy of the Canadian National Railways Magazine of June, 1930, which contains a picture of Sir Henry Thornton laying the corner stone of the new railway station in Hamilton. On that occasion he said:
This new station, of which I have the honour to lay the corner stone, is but a vision of the past come true; and it is a permanent testimonial of the work that has been done. It is true that there is no such thing as satisfaction, completion, or finish, for achievement only spurs us to greater endeavour and to greater progress. Therefore, to you veterans I can only say "thank you" and tell you that you have made traditions of which we are all proud and which we hope to emulate in the future.
This is a nice speech for the laying of the corner stone of a station.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think perhaps the hon. gentleman had better delete that reference from his remarks; it is not in order to introduce the name of the Governor General.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not referring to the Governor General; I am referring to Sir Henry Thornton. To proceed with the station at Riviere du Loup, two ministers of the crown said the Conservative candidate had worked hard for that station. I asked them questions and found that the. Solicitor General left for the Imperial conference on September 23 and returned on December 12, and he said he had not in the meantime communicated by letter, wireless, cablegram or wireless telephone with any person in connection with the proposed construction of the new railway station at Riviere du Loup. This answer of the Solicitor General appears in Hansard of June 5. The answer of the Minister of Railways, which appeared in Hansard of May 2S, stated that he left Ottawa op October 1
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot

and' oame back on October 11, and in the meantime did not communioate with anyone with regard to the proposed new station. The other ministers whom the Tory candidate met in Ottawa on October 7 last were the Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve), the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart), and when I asked them for information they refused to answer, because they said, of their oath of office. The hon. member for Argon-teuil (Sir George Perley) was appointed acting Minister of Railways on October 7, by order in council. On March 31 I asked the following question, which appears in Hansard:
Was he appointed acting Minister of Railways in order to refuse to sanction the construction work at Riviere du Loup?
Mr. Manion: Certainly not.
That was a good answer, but on the very day of his appointment as acting minister the Canadian National Railways returned the cheque to the tenderers, saying the Department of Railways and Canals had refused to sanction the construction of the station. That, was while the Solicitor General and the Minister of Railways were out of Ottawa, and both of them pretty far away. On June 1 I asked this question:
What was: (a) the date; (b) the number: (c) the subject matter of each.order in council submitted to him while acting as such, to the privy council during that period?
The answer was that there was one order in council dated October 8, 1930, in fact October 9, P.C. 2370, with regard to orders for an addition to the station at Levis, Quebec. He refused to sanction the construction of a station at Riviere du Loup, though he was not appointed to do so, and in fact he approved of an addition to another station at a place no more important than Riviere du Loup. Through the courtesy of the Prime Minister I have a copy of that order in council, and I wonder whether, on the recommendation of the new board of directors of the Canadian National Railways, the money voted by parliament for the station at Riviere du Loup was spent in virtue of an order in council on the addition to the station at Levis.
I do not wish to be rude to any hon. member of the house, but on April 16 last, at page 650 of Hansard, an hon. member accused me of playing vaudeville with the station at Riviere du Loup. I am sorry the right hon. Prime Minister has left the chamber, but I will ask the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes) to convey my message to him. That very same hon. member was on the train with me one day going from Ottawa to Montreal and he said, "I am {Mr. Pouliot.]
. very sorry I cannot speak English; otherwise I would tell these facts to the government." I mention no name, but anyone referring to Hansard will realize whom I am speaking of. It is pretty hard to speak both ways in and outside of the house. Take for example, Mr. Speaker, a respectable Conservative paper like the Mail and Empire. What does that paper say on June 10 with reference to the photographs of Riviere du Loup station, laid on the table of the house? Let me quote;
The photos, he stated in an interview to-day, show what words cannot bring. They make clear, he said, the holes in the present station's roof and the way the water runs into the waiting room from a flanking hillside every time it rains-and it rains plenty in Riviere du Loup.
If Mr. Pouliot is able to table the pictures, as he claims is his right, without being ruled out of order, no member of the house, he declared, will be able to plead ignorance of the true state of affairs beside the tracks at Riviere du Loup.
I have here the correspondence that has been laid on the table under reference No. 242, the correspondence exchanged between the Minister of Railways and the Conservative candidate. The file is not complete: some of the letters are here but others are missing. No letter from that gentleman to the minister is produced, the explanation being that it is marked personal. I believe I have sufficient time to read one of the letters not marked personal-and I would observe, by the way, that one wonders what the personal letters must be like. This letter, which is a translation, reads:
Riviere du Loup,
January 17, 1931.
Mr. Arthur Lalonde,
Secretary,
Post Office Department.
Dear Sir,
Re: Isle Verte R.R. No. 1 This mail service has been asked by Mr. J. F. Pouliot, before the elections, it has been granted, mail contract awarded, more than 50 per cent of the residents have bought boxes.

Chs. E. Dube.
I protest against any communication of that character for it is utterly false and unjust for the civil servants.

The Budget-Mr. Nicholson
A communication from the Minister of Railways to the clerk of the city of Riviere du Loup on November 6 was to this effect: "Your city was not proposed in a special way when the question was presented." This means everything, because the Conservative candidate was in Ottawa when the question was decided by the acting minister.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I submit that my county has been discriminated against. The reason is obvious: they wanted to punish the good electors who voted for the Liberal candidate. But they did not realize that at the same time they were punishing their own friends. The gentleman to whom I have referred, the Conservative candidate, wrote an article in his own name, in Saint Laurent, in October last, in which he made this statement: "I have not been elected; I have no promises to fulfil." That will give the house an idea of the way in which my constituency has been treated. I have been asking for returns to orders made in this house, and I have got some crumbs from the table of the rich, for which I am thankful. May I suggest that a square meal would be welcome-all the orders I have been asking for. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote the following excerpt from May's Parliamentary Practice, twelfth edition, page 564:
If parties neglect to make returns in reasonable time, they are ordered to make them forthwith: or so much of returns as lxas not been made. If they continue to withhold them, they are ordered to attend at the bar of the house; and unless they satisfactorily explain the causes of their neglect, and comply with the order of the house, they will be censured or punished according to the circumstances of the case.
I wish to be lenient, but at the same time I desire to have at the earliest possible date the answers which I have been expecting. I shall be thankful to the government when they bring down these returns, and I am sure that when they realize the true facts of the situation they will be disgusted with the local Tory tactics in my county and will put a stop to the present state of affairs.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In rising to address the house briefly on the resolution proposed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), it is not my purpose to discuss at length more than one subject, and that is the effort that is being made throughout the country and in this house to fasten on the government and on the Conservative party the charge of endeavouring to undermine the Canadian National Railways. In dealing with this matter I intend to put before the house some information which I think will convince all reasonable people that 22110-164
it is the men on this side of the house, and those who are willing to examine closely into Ihe expenditures of the Canadian National Railways, in order to ascertain exactly what the position is and what circumstances have led up to the present situation, who are in reality the friends of the system itself.
The Canadian National Railways came into existence as a result of a situation with which this country was confronted in 1917, 1918 and 1919-a situation brought about by the fact that the parliament of Canada had utterly failed in its duty in the years from 1904 up until that time. I am not going to weary the house by traversing everything that took place. I am not going to endeavour to fasten upon one political party or the other responsibility for that situation. The fact remains that it was the parliament of Canada, as a parliament, by reason of its docile attitude to the proposals put before it, proposals in themselves utterly and completely unsound, that placed us in a position, in those years I have mentioned, 1917, 1918 and 1919, which compelled us to take over the roads and endeavour to amalgamate them into one system.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) in the course of this debate, referred to one or two matters which I shall consider. The- hon. gentleman referred to securities in the long-term bonded indebtedness of the Canadian National Railways which he said dated back to 1875 and some of them, I believe he said, to 1850. And the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), referring to the sum of 8604,000,000 in the balance sheet of the Canadian National Railways for 1930, representing direct advances by the government of Canada, stated that those advances were made prior to the taking-over and amalgamation of the lines. Before I conclude I shall endeavour to show the fallacy of these two statements.
I have in my hand a copy of the Toronto Globe of Saturday, June 6, 1931, in which there is an article that illustrates the campaign that has been going on all over the country since August last in relation to these railways. This editorial is headed, "The Inquisition Under Way," and there appears in it this statement:
Premier Bennett in his budget speech provided a text for the special committee on national railways and shipping, which has commenced a probe of Canadian National affairs.
Now, that special committee on railways and shipping is the representative body of this house which is inquiring into details of expenditures made by the Canadian National

The Budget-Mr. Nicholson

Railways, which expenditures are to be covered by direct vote of this parliament. Yet, referring to that committee, the Toronto Globe, in an article indicative of what is talcing place throughout the country, taking its cue from statements made by hon. members in this house, describes the work of the committee as an inquisition, because before voting millions and tens of millions of dollars parliament presumes to make an inquiry as to what this money is being spent for or why it is asked for.
Let me say at once that so far as I am concerned, and so long as I remain in this house, I intend if I can to find out why parliament is asked to vote money for any purpose whatsoever; and I intend particularly, if I can, to ascertain why it is that so much money is required for this enterprise we call the Canadian National Railways. I conceive it to be the duty of every member of this house, the friends of the. system itself, to go the extreme limit in finding out what the position is, suggesting if they can the remedy, and paying special attention to the expenditures that are now being made and the sums which are asked for.
I 'have in my hand the balance sheet for 1030 of the Canadian National Railways, and it shows the total liabilities as $2,531,000,000 in round figures; it shows that there have been approximately $1,350,000,000 added to the liabilities of the system since the lines were taken over in ioi7, 1018 and 1019. Reverting for a moment to the statement made by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yar-mouth regarding the long-term funded debt dating back to 1875, I would say that a statement of that character made by whomsoever it may be is merely an effort to throw sand in the eyes of the Canadian people.
hen the Canadian Northern lines were taken over by the Canadian people the value was fixed by arbitration, and that value was such that the obligation assumed was $384,000,000 in round figures. The common stock, representing the investment of those who were behind the railway, of a par value of $100,000,000, was wiped out entirely with the exception of $10,000,000.
When the Grand Trunk Railway was taken over under the legislation of 1010, there were approximately $211,000,000 of securities wiped out as being of no value. I have before me the total cost of these lines, including the cost of the Transcontinental and the Intercolonial railways, which cost is $1,106,237,620.72.
