subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. From the Montreal Star of June 6 I quote the following:
With vast numbers walking the streets of the city in search of jobs there can be no mistake that Montreal is face to face with a grave crisis. Stark poverty and wretchedness is the lot of hundreds, maybe thousands, in the midst of a city whose reputation for organized charitable effort is acknowledged all over Canadji. Once again it becomes vitally necessary to plan ways and means of relieving the hungry and homeless sufferers. To enable the unmarried man who is genuinely seeking work to go on hoping, to save him from the bitter thought of utter defeat, prompt action is absolutely necessary.
As regards Vancouver, I know what the conditions were like there last year, for I was closely connected with the unemployment situation. The following is from the Province of June 5:
"Well, we are rapidly approaching a financial crisis," said Alderman Bennett. "When these 1,400 men are laid off this month it will mean we have 3,000 families to keep. Unless one or both governments come to our aid, it means a bank overdraft or having to close up shop."
Last year we did not have 3,000 families on unemployment relief at this time of the year. That would represent from 12,000 to 15,000 persons. But let us take the city of Ottawa. In the Citizen of yesterday, I find the following report:
A round-up by city police yesterday afternoon of the rat-ridden hovels netted 69 unem ployed men, who were brought to police headquarters and placed in custody on vagrancy charges.
The round-up followed complaints from residents of Ottawa east. Six trips were made by the police patrol to bring in the men, who instead of being placed in cells were turned loose in the cell corridor. According to Deputy Chief Gilhooly it is likely that the men will not be arraigned in police court but will be given their liberty this morning. Following the arrests the police purchased four dozen loaves of bread, and a contribution of bologna and cheese was later sent to the police station. Then to complete a meal for the unfortunates the_ authorities ordered ten gallons of coffee which was delivered at the police station. This raised the spirits of the prisoners, some of whom said they hadn't had a square meal for a considerable time.
It did not require a great deal to raise their spirits.
The meal provided by the police at least surpassed what some of the men had intended for their supper before their arrest. As if some of them had been disturbed in the preparation of their meals, here and there food, some of it with the appearance of having been picked

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
up in the dump, remained lying around when a Citizen reporter visited the dump last night.
Take next the evening edition of the same paper:
Homeless Men Get Police Sympathy Building for Dogs to Replace Shacks Inhabited . by Transients	.
While detectives were in the city engineering department arranging for the demolition of shacks on city property, the Lees avenue dump, which had housed three or four score unfortunate men, an officer of Ottawa Humane Society was in the same office to submit plans for a' $10,000 building to be erected on city property for the care of dogs.
. It is proposed to erect the Humane Society building on part of the Broad street corporation vard in the opposite end of the scity to the city dump where the men established themselves in make-shift shacks. Even the_ officers and men wiio arranged for the demolition ot shacks expressed the opinion that until better provision were made for the men they should be allowed to continue in the shacks so long as they did not molest or offend others.
I see by the Evening Journal of the same date that the police have announced their intention of making periodical visits to the dump and vicinity in the future, to forestall settlement there. Surely these are wonderful conditions, when the police have to guard the city's dump to keep Canadians from making their domicile there. Yet my hon. friend says that conditions are not as bad as they were last year. Let me read a question which was put to Sir Henry Thornton in the railway committee yesterday. The question was asked by the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson).
What did the railway intend to do about falling revenues, asked R. B. Hanson. Conservative member for York-Sunbury. "In view of the alarming conditions, what does the road intend to do?" he repeated. Revenues of the road-for the first part of June dropped 25 per cent, and "things are worse now than they were in 1930."
"You are quite correct, and I share your alarm," replied Sir Henry, "but frankly I do not know the answer to your question. Perhaps it should be addressed to the prophets of Israel. We cannot announce what we are going to do because we do not know."
And I presume the government is in the same position. But while the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the election campaign .was seized -with the seriousness of the situation, he was quite moderate in his language in comparison with his leader. I do not think he said that they were going to end unemployment; I feel sure he did not. But the present Prime Minister, speaking in Regina on June 10, and as reported in the Daily Province of June 11, said:
I never in all my life saw- such unemployment in this Canada of ours as in this year of 1930. . . . Canada is blessed with great natural resources; yet we find something which

saddened my heart to-day. I met men wearing the white button of the unemployed, and all they ask is a chance to work.
It was in June, 1930, when the hon. gentleman's heart was saddened, but, as I said before, there are more unemployed to-day in June, 1931, in every city in Canada than there was in June, 1930, and yet there is no mention in the budget of relief for unemployment.
I was wondering who went to the trouble of obtaining the white badges for the unem-ploj'ed in Regina in June last. It was not the labour or the communist parties because in that case the buttons would have been red, or at least pale pink; it was not the Liberal party, because there were no unemployed last year, and they would not buy buttons for anybody. I do not think it was the farmers because they had not the price. That cuts down the list of those who might have purchased those buttons, and I leave the house to conjecture just who it was.
Since last year it has been found expedient for the government to realize that world economic conditions have a bearing on the economic conditions prevailing in this country, and that it was not all due to the fiscal policy of the preceding government. I have quoted these statements to show where the party in power stood when in opposition, when the conditions of unemployment were not as serious as they are to-day. A few days ago I gave to the house the unemployment figures for Vancouver; the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has given the figures for Vancouver island, and the hon. members for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) have given the figures for Winnipeg. A few moments ago the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) mentioned what had been done last year, but I feel that any proposals which the government may make should be made in sufficient time to enable this house to consider them. He stated, as I quoted a few moments ago, that two-thirds of the unemployed who had to be kept by the city of Vancouver were from outside the city. The unemployment figures for October 31 show that the total unemployed in Canada amounted to 47,682; the figure for British Columbia was 8.581, and for Vancouver. 4.712. It will be noticed that the city of Vancouver had well over half of the total unemployed in the province of British Columbia; that British Columbia had 18 per cent of the total unemployed in Canada, and Vancouver, *9-86 per cent of the total. Based upon these figures British Columbia was entitled to 18 per cent of the federal grant, or $2,880,000, when in fact it was allocated $900,000 or 5-6 per cent. On

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
the basis of unplaced applicants on October 31, the, cjty of Vancouver was entitled to 9-86 per cent, or SI,577,600, when in fact it received 1-3 per cent or $220,000, approximately one. eighth of its just proportion, or a shortage of SI,356,600. That is one of the reasons why I, at least, want to know in good time what the government has in mind and what proposals it intends to make in connection with unemployment.
Canada is a country possessed of great natural wealth and wealth in usable form, and yet we are told that there must be retrenchment, that strict economy must be practised. What does strict economy mean as far as the working class is concerned? They are economizing all the time. Strict economy on the part of this government will mean less work and more unemployment; strict economy will mean more hunger, more destitution, more . want, more disease, more crime, more insanity, more suicides and more human deterioration.
An lion, MEMBER:	Does the hon. member want the country to go bankrupt?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is quite possible that
we might go bankrupt in figures, but we would not be bankrupt in actual wealth. Economy- when we have our trade commissioners in every country of the world trying to dispose of our surplus products, and there are in this country the trade agents of other countries trying to dispose of their surpluses. Economy -when millions of bushels of wheat and other grains are rotting in the elevators of this country.

speechtext: Who is responsible?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
Who is responsible, this
government?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Trotzky.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, not even Trotzky. No one is responsible just at the moment, but someone will be responsible unless we take heed of what is actually transpiring and take time by the forelock and put our house in order before a general collapse occurs. I do not place the blame on anyone, but the blame may be and will be placed on someone, and those on whom the blame is placed will have to bear it.
Economy-when clothing is being moth-eaten and becoming shopworn in our stores and warehouses, when lumber is rotting in
the woods and in the mills, when foodstuffs are allowed to spoil and have to be destroyed beca.use they cannot be used. Economy- when hundreds of thousands of people are ready to work to produce more as needed.
The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young), who preceded me, laid these ills at the door of the tariff. I am neither a high tariff nor low tariff man as I think the tariff has little effect upon our economic system; at the best it is only a negative policy. In a world where the worker must make a profit for someone else, where he must produce more than he receives in wages, there is bound to be a surplus. If the employees in one industry cannot consume the goods produced therein, then the employees of all industries cannot consume their products. So that you have a piling up of goods, not because there are not wants to be filled, but because the people who produce these goods have not the purchasing power to buy them back. That is one of the causes of our difficulties.
I want to quote a few figures from the statistics of the Department of Labour as recorded in the Canada Year Book, covering the years from 1920 to 1828. They show that the index of productive efficiency of wage earners increased from 97-0 in 1920 to 148-5 in 1928, while the real value of wages increased only from 100-4 in 1920 to 116-4 in 1928. In productive efficiency there is a gain of 51-5 per cent, while in the real value of wages there has been an increase of only 16 per cent. Now let us see where this increase of 35-5 per cent in volume of production over the real value of wages went. The capital invested in Canada in 1920 was $3,371,000,000 and in 1928, $4,780,000,000, an increase of 42 per cent. Wages and salaries in the same period increased from $732,120,000 in 1920 to $755,199,000 in 1928, an increase of 3 per cent. If you have an increase of 42 per cent in capital and an increase of only 3 per cent in wages, how are you going to consume your total production? What are you going to do? There are all kinds of needs and all kinds of work to be done in this country, but there is no gainful employment out of which a profit can be made from the labour of the worker, and if that cannot be found the people will be unemployed.
An hon. gentleman on the other side of the house a few moments ago asked who was responsible for all this. I said that I was not blaming anybody. I should like, however, in this connection to quote from a speech made by Sir George Paish in New York a few days ago, as reported by the New York Times of June 9, 1931. I think his remarks are well

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
worth reading and thinking over; he is a greater authority than I am. I quote:
Sir George predicted greater distress in America and in other countries in this coming winter "than we have witnessed in modern times" and urged timely preparation of relief measures. He advocated unemployment insurance as the only means of averting revolution in countries which, like Great Britain, had been suffering from chronic unemployment.
Personally I would not advocate unemployment insurance merely for the sake of averting revolution, but I am quite sure that it has done that much at least in the British isles. Not only has it done that, but in Great Britain they have come thus far through the depression with less lowering of their standard of living than any other country in the world to-day. I quote again:
The belief that next winter will bring more acute distress was shared by officials of the Welfare Council, which represent the principal welfare and health agencies of the city.
"1 am also very much disturbed," said Sir George "about the situation in the world, and it is clear that both you and we, in fact all countries, will be up against a good deal. In a measure we are going to fight probably the greatest peace battle that we have fought. You will remember that during the war we were right up against it. We had to mobilize all our forces to win the war. Now we have to mobilize the forces of every possible kind to win this fight against trade depression. Indeed, if I may say so. in my judgment there is a danger, a great danger, of a complete breakdown of trade, and we must be prepared. If those who are able to control world affairs are wise and act rvisely, then we may mitigate the disaster. It cannot be prevented."
Those are the words of Sir George Paish. He continues:
"It can only be made bearable."
He is not the only one who is beginning to feel that the situation is getting very precarious indeed. I continue to quote:
Sir George said that the politicians and statesmen must bear the responsibility: "They have done everything in their power, they desired to do everything in their power to hamper trade," he said. "They have increased tariffs, they have imposed embargoes, they have created licences; in fact, they have left nothing undone to hamper trade. I wish to compliment the politicians and statesmen of the world on the success of their policy. They have left nothing undone to hamper the trade of the world and to bring ruin. They have succeeded, but it means the suicide of the world. I am not saying that of New York, but of my country and of every country. It is essential that people should realize the danger in which they are. the danger of the complete breakdown of trade bringing unparalleled distress. This is no mere trade depression. It is a catastrophe of the first moment."
The report continues:
The world's great misfortune had been, Sir George added, that each nation was trying to solve the problem in its own narrow, national
[Mr. Maclnnis.1
way, whan as a matter of fact the problem required common action.
"Each nation has been trying to get ^out, thinking that its problem is a local one," he said. "This has carried us into deeper and deeper distress. This problem is not merely a national problem. It is essential that every nation in the world should cooperate with every other nation to get the world out of distress. The world problem must be faced by the world."
Lastly Sir George Paish said:
AVe must each of us stand for the welfare of the other nations. AVe have to create a condition in the world that will make all nations prosperous. Out of world prosperity our own prosperity will follow.
The Prime Minister in concluding his budget speech said that we must have faith, courage and determination. It is all right to have faith, and it is easy to have courage and determination when your stomach is full and you have a place to live and sleep, but it is going a little too far to tell the unemployed, who are citizens of this country, that they must have faith. They have come to the time when hope, deferred, maketh the heart, sick.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr Speaker, taking part for the first time in a debate in this house I wish to point out to the government some of the difficulties that, confront the people of the constituency of Maple Creek, which I have the honour to represent. In doing so I am not unmindful of other parts of the country. Maple Creek is situated in the southwestern portion of the province of Saskatchewan, bordered by Alberta to the west and the state of Montana to the south. It is purely agricultural, and although there are large areas where mixed farming is carried on, wheat growing is the major industry.
I wish to extend my congratulations to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) upon the budget he presented to this house. I wish also to thank him for the consideration extended to the western farmers. I may say I have had many letters from the west commending the recent budget. There will be no attempt on my part, Mr. Speaker, to disguise the fact that at the present time conditions in -western Canada are exceedingly trying and difficult. Those opposed to us who have sought to emphasize this condition should however not forget their silence of just a few short months ago when conditions were exceedingly bad and drifting with startling rapidity to the state of affairs which exist to-day. At that time hon. members opposite did not think it necessary to paint a dismal picture or to call attention to the swift and disastrous declension that was taking

The Budget-Mr. Swnnston
place in agricultural Canada, especially in the prairie west. Canada occupies almost one-halt of the northern agricultural area of the world. The rest of the far northern hemisphere is almost wholly in the hands of Russia. Consequently, Canada is brought into first and direct competition with a country which is now operating under a new and peculiar form of despotism, which form of government for the time being at least enjoys the fanatical support of most of the vast millions of the Russian population. While this enthusiasm continues and while those vast millions are ready to sacrifice every comfort and many of the necessities of life in the belief that they are building up an earthly paradise to come, the nature of the competition which now faces Canada can well be imagined. This is the competition against which the Canadian farmers are now pitted, and in the struggle they merit and demand the practical cooperation of the Canadian government and the Canadian people, and unless such cooperation is given the Canadian farmer can remain in competition only by reduoing his standard of living to the level of that obtaining in Russia. I do not say that these melancholy conditions can by any sort of reasoning be considered permanent, but I fear that in the present state of mind of the Russian people such a condition may actually exist, and it is with these and near future troubles we now have to contend. The complaisance of the Russian people, despite the tyranny under which they live and the deplorable standards of living of the peasants, constitutes the real problem Canadians have to face to-day.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend keeps on talking there will be no doubt as to my being returned at the next election.
I represent an area in the west which is not exclusively wheat growing but to some extent is interested in mixed farming. The constituency of Maple Creek has long been noted for its production of cattle, horses, sheep and hogs, in wheat Russian competition is imminent and its effect is crushing. In the cattle trade competition is coming, but I do not anticipate it will be quite as severe as it will be in the case of wheat.' As long as the Canadian farmer is called upon to compete
with free labour only he has courage to face such competition, and in the past he has always been able to succeed. Russian labour, is not free labour. For the time being a great deal of the labour may be voluntary and sacrifices are willingly borne because of promises of future glory. Actually, however, the condition is one of forced labour in one sphere after another of Russian activity and the result is that the Canadian farmer should and must have special . protection in the world's markets. This applies to all free farming communities in all parts of the world, and especially in the British Empire. It should be the duty of the statesmen of this empire to see that such protection is given. In turn Canada should be ready to give advantages to other countries, especially to the mother country, in return for the advantages given in their market against the product of the forced labour of Russia. All classes of people should be prepared to see that trade arrangements are made which will bring about special advantage to Canada in the British market as well as in the other markets of the world. Surely we have not come to the time when under the influence of a wild and fantastic mania any country in the world can dictate the standards of living which must prevail in other countries. It is the function of this government to protect the standard of living, and the Canadian people expect this government not to fail. All through these years the Canadian farmer has done his share to maintain the standards of living of the workmen, manufacturers and financiers. Now the workmen, manufacturers and financiers along with all other classes in Canada must indeed do their part to maintain the standard of living of the Canadian agriculturist. I compliment the government upon having already taken action along this line. What has been done has been only a step, but it has placed Canada in a position to proceed with treaty negotiations which will be in the interest of our farmers.
As I have seen other hon. members referring to notes Mr. Speaker, I shall take that liberty. One of the chief difficulties with which we in Maple Creek constituency are faced is the lack of railway facilities. A few days ago when the railway estimates were before this house I observed, when it became known that the railway officials of the Canadian National Railways had decided to curtail the expenses by making a out in certain lines which were not paying costs of operation, that some hon. members representing the constituencies affected appealed to the Minister of Railways and Canals to maintain those lines even at a loss to the Canadian

The Budget-Mr. Swamlon
National Railways and to the country. What would be the attitude of hon. members, if, instead of 'having a curtailed railway service, they had no railway at all? In Maple Creek constituency there are large stretches of fertile country that have no railway. The residents of those districts are the most thrifty and the finest class of people in the world. They have waited a long time for a railroad. They have paid heavy taxes for many years. They have sent petitions and requests to the railway officials and to the government. They have hauled their wheat and other farm products over long trails for many years, and on top of that they have paid extra freight and express charges. They are greatly handicapped on account of lack of railway transportation facilities to the market. Those people are not asking for a daily train service; all they are asking for is a railway to help them to reduce the cost of production and transportation at this time when the prices of farm products are so low.
To encourage those people to stay on the land, to give them some hope of success in the future and to furnish employment to the unemployed, I am going to appeal to the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) and to the government to use their influence with the officials of the Canadian Pacific railway to hasten the construction of the following lines: The gap between Mankota and Val-marie; the Dunelm-Vesper extension; the Verio extension, and the extension from Golden Prairie to Big Stick lake. I shall not take up the time of the house in explaining all the inconveniences experienced by the people in those districts, but I should like to mention one gap, that is on the south line, between Mankota and Valmarie. Travelling east from Valmarie or any of the towns west of the gap, you will first travel one day west to Consul, then spend another day travelling east to Shaunavon on the Weyburn-Lethbridge line, and after travelling for two days, you are now thirty-ffive miles north and thirty-five miles further west than you were when you started two days previously. Thus hon. members will see the need of the construction of these lines.
Just a word with reference to the Hudson Bay railway. A few days ago the Prime Minister, announced that the grain rates on the Hudson Bay railway, when it was placed in operation, would be based on the Crows-nest pass rates. This is welcome news to the people of western Canada. The western farmer will make a great saving on both his wheat and cattle. It is estimated by good authority that the saving on wheat will 
be from 7 to 8 cents a bushel,, or in the neighbourhood of $100 per car. To ship a carload of cattle from Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan, to Montreal. costs $221 per car of 20,000 pounds, while to ship the same car to Churchill would cost $108, or a saving of $113 per car. In addition to the cash saving, there, will be an economic advantage, in that less feed and less care will be necessary in shipping to Churchill and the cool northern route will be easier on the cattle so that there will be diminished shrinkage. In the case of dairy products going to the British Isles, it is estimated that a shipper from Regina will save $190 on a car of butter by shipping by way of Churchill, and the savings on shipments from other parts of Saskatchewan will be in proportion. I congratulate the Minister of Railways for hastening the construction of this line.
Probably one of the most significant developments which have taken place recently, at least so far as Canada is concerned, is the reappearance of Russia in the world's wheat market, and Russian competition in the marketing of this commodity may well be viewed with concern. In 1930 more than 200,000,000 bushels of Russian wheat were offered in competition with Canadian wheat in the British market. In 1928 Argentina had a wheat crop of 350,000,000 bushels, or 129,000,000 bushels above her average for the years 1923 to 1927. She also held, at the beginning of the Canadian crop year 1929-30, in round numbers, 120,000,000 bushels available for export as compared with 61,000,000 bushels, the average during the years 1923 to 1927, and, moreover, no one in Canada seemed to have any idea of this enormous increase in the wheat crops of Russia and Argentina. Here were two countries sending tens of millions of bushels of unsold wheat to sea and dumping it on the market wherever possible at greatly reduced prices and greatly below the cost of production. When these large shipments of distressed wheat neared the shores of such countries as Germany, France, Italy and Spain, they found protective tariff Walls over which they could not sell. Those countries had decided to protect the home markets for their home grown wheat. Consequently those ships turned their course to Britain, and unloaded their wheat at any available price, displacing Canadian wheat.
No information had reached western Canada from the ex-Minister of Trade and Com*-merce regarding the serious condition of the wheat market. No information was received from the marketing experts of the Liberal government to inform the western farmer of the danger of holding his wheat, when the British

The Budget-Mr. Swanston
market was. being crammed to its utmost capacity with wheat from Russia, Argentina and other countries. Surely it was. the duty of the intelligence department to keep the wheat grower advised when such serious conditions arose. After hearing that the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce had made the statement that the wheat market would take care of itself, it was no surprise to me to hear that wheat markets had been lost. And may I say right at this point that it is much easier to lose markets than it is to find them. If timely information had been given the wheat growers of Canada, our wheat would have been sold and an extra $100,000,000 would have been distributed among the farmers of western Canada. Instead of that, the wheat has been held in the elevators and the farmers have spent their last dollar to pay elevator charges and other expenses. Although every effort is being made to leave the impression throughout the country that this administration has been unable to find markets for our wheat, the fact, remains that our exports of wheat are increasing. Let us see exactly what has happened. In July, 1929, the price of wheat was $1.78 per bushel' while in July, 1930, before this government came into office, it had dropped to S7 cents per bushel. During the crop year ending July, 1930, we exported 155,000,000 bushels of wheat. During the first ten months of this year we have exported 195,000,000 bushels, and the booking estimates for June and July, the last of the crop year, is 234,000,000 bushels, or an increase of 80,000,000 bushels this year as against last year under our fiscal policy. France took 9,800,000 bushels this year as against 6,000,000 bushels last year. This would seem to indicate that markets are being found.
The farmers of western Canada must look for a reduction in -the prices of farm implements and gasoline, for a reduction in freight rates and for lower interest rates on loans. The absorption by the government of five cents per bushel in connection with the cost of transportation of wheat will assist the farmer to the extent of $15,000,000 or more a year in normal times, and this provision is made effective this year.
With reference to the banks and financial institutions, I am of the opinion that the banks, loan companies, implement companies and other financial institutions should not be allowed to charge over 7 per cent on their loans. I believe agriculture in western Canada cannot be developed on a sound economic basis under high interest rates. I am greatly concerned over the mounting debt of the fanners in our part of the country, due to interest on farm loans and interest owing implement companies. I believe the farmers are honest
and do not wish to evade their debts, but-their honesty is being stretched to the point of breaking because under present conditions their debt is growing out of all proportion to their ability to pay.
To keep the farmer on his land I would suggest a conference of representatives of the farmers, the municipal councils, the provincial governments, the banks, the implement companies, the loan companies and the federal government in order to see if something cannot be done to assist in adjusting -this debt and giving the farmer a fresh start. This: will pay best in the long run. It would seem as though some of this debt must be adjusted in order to give the farmers of the west a chance. They cannot pay these high interest rates much longer.	;
In view of the fact that there has been a good deal of discussion with regard to the effect of the Australian treaty on the dairy industry of Canada, I have secured from the bureau of statistics the figures with regard to the exports and imports of butter during the five years the treaty was in operation. The exports were as follows:

The six months' notice ending the treaty became effective in the middle of October, and in the following month, after the treaty was cancelled, we imported only 124,943 pounds. Apparently every effort was made by those shipping butter into Canada to ship in as much a3 possible before the abrogation of the treaty in the middle of October.
To summarize the actual situation during the five years of the treaty, Canada, one of the most important dairy producing countries in the world, exporting butter at the rate of 26,000,000 pounds annually in 1925, exported only a little more than 1,000,000 pounds in 1930, and our imports increased from 99,000 pounds in 1925 to the enormous figure of over 47,000,000 pounds in 1930. other words, in 1930 we exported twenty-five times less butter than in 1925, and imported 470 times as much. During this period our exports of milk and cream diminished by 75 per cent and our exports of cheese were cut in two. Our dairy farmers were so greatly affected by the treaty that many milch cows were sold for beef, reducing our dairy herds by over 100,000 cows. In the small town of Hatton, in the constituency of Maple Creek, in July, 1925, the heaviest cream month of the year, they shipped 350 cans of cream a week. During the same month in 1929 the number of cans had been reduced to less than 100 per week. The farmers of that town lost thousands of dollars through the large importations of New Zealand butter.
This leads me to say a few words with reference to the bacon industry, because when there is a diminished production in dairy products there will be a falling off in the bacon trade, as those two industries run hand in hand. Previous to the Australian treaty we were exporting 220,000,000 pounds of bacon annually, but by 1930, this was reduced to 20,000,000 pounds.
My time is almost up. I should have liked to say something with regard to the tariff and the income tax, but I will leave those matters for another occasion.
